# Cost fixtures

Input for `make cost-check`, the gate over `scripts/fold-cost.py` (ADR-0045).

## These are hand-written, and that is the right call here — unlike next door

`tests/fixtures/timeline/` makes the opposite argument in its own README, and
both are correct, because the two gates are aimed at different things.

`fold-timeline.py` folds **Terraform's** event schema. A fixture invented from a
reading of the documentation would test its author's belief about that schema,
which is why every stream in that directory is real terraform output.

`fold-cost.py` reads the timeline this project already produced — **our** schema,
folded and gated one layer down. What it has to be exercised against is not "what
does terraform emit" but "what does a cycle look like when it goes wrong": a
teardown that missed something, a destroy paired with the wrong apply, an
environment still up. Waiting for a real cycle to leave each of those behind
would mean waiting for six failures that cost money.

So the timestamps carry the weight, and one case's are not invented at all.

## `a-lifetime-is-not-a-creation` is a real cycle, transcribed

Every instant in it comes from the published timelines of the cycle of
2026-08-08 — apply `31276975666`, destroy `31277877190`, stage. Nothing was
rounded and nothing was arranged:

```text
aws_lb              created in 173s, then stood for 1582 more
aws_db_instance     created in 297s, then stood for  852
aws_ecs_service     created in   1s, then stood for 1143
```

That is the case for the whole file. An estimate multiplying `elapsed_seconds`
by a rate would have reported a ninth of the load balancer's real cost and would
have looked completely reasonable doing it.

## The rates are synthetic and say so

`rates.json` here is not AWS pricing and must never be read as any. Its figures
are round so the arithmetic in `expected.json` can be checked by hand:
3.6 USD/hour is exactly 0.001 USD/second, so the ALB's 1582 seconds cost 1.582.
The real table is captured by `scripts/fetch-rates.py` into `site/data/rates.json`
and carries the SKU and filters behind every figure.

The **shape** is a fixture too — `shape.json` in each case, rather than a read of
`infra/`. The gate is over the fold, not over the configuration; coupling it to
live variable defaults would mean a task-size change reddening a case about
teardown leftovers. `make rates-check` is what watches the configuration.

## The cases

```text
a-lifetime-is-not-a-creation                the real cycle, above
the-ten-minute-minimum-binds-on-a-short-    a database deleted two minutes after
  cycle                                     it came up still costs ten. The one
                                            direction a duration-only fold can
                                            never go: UP
an-open-cycle-is-priced-to-an-instant       no destroy timeline. The meter is
                                            open, every row says so
a-kind-nobody-classified-is-unpriced        a NAT gateway the cost model has
                                            never heard of - UNPRICED and loud,
                                            not folded in as a zero
a-delete-with-no-create-is-named            the destroy removed something this
                                            apply never created: the symptom of
                                            a destroy paired with the wrong apply
a-resource-the-teardown-never-touched       the leftover class of ADR-0041, seen
                                            from the money side. Its meter does
                                            not stop at the teardown
```

`expected.json` is committed and compared, never regenerated by the gate. There
is no `--bless` flag on purpose: a gate that rewrites its own expectations
records what the code did rather than what it should do.
